Āternĭus.opening: a Roman family name : Aternius Fontinalis, a consul A. U. C. 300, Cic. Rep. 2, 35, 60 Mai; from him proceeded the Lex Aternia (or Tarpeia; cf. Fest. s. v. peculatus, p. 237 Müll.): de multā, Gell. 11, 1, 2 .

Ā^tlantĭgĕna.opening: Atlas-gigno , begotten of Atlas , daughter of Atlas , i. e. Maia; old poet in Anthol. Lat. Burm. 2, p. 364 .

ātrāmentārĭum.opening: atramentum , an inkstand : atramentarium scriptoris, Vulg. Ezech. 9, 2 (as transl. of the Heb. ); 9, 3; 9, 11.

ātrāmentum.opening: ater , any black liquid : sepiae, Cic. N D. 2, 50, 127 . Writing-ink , ink; in Vitr. 7, 10 , and Plin. 27, 7, 28, § 52 , called atramentum librarium: calamo et atramento temperato, Cic. ad Q. Fr. 2, 15, 6 : per…

ātrātus.opening: P. a. , as if from atro, āre [ater], clothed in black for mourning , dressed in mourning : cedo, quis umquam cenārit atratus? * Cic. Vatin. 12 fin. : plebes, Tac. A. 3, 2 : senex, Suet. Galb. 18 .— Also of suppliants:…

Ā^trax.opening: , = Ἄτραξ . Masc. , a river in Ætolia , Plin. 4, 2, 3, § 6 .— Derivv. , those living near the Atrax , Plin. 4, 2, 3, § 6 .— , , adj. , of Atrax , Atracian : oris, Prop. 1, 8, 25 (Müll., Antariis ).— Fem. , a town in…

ātrĭŏlum.opening: dim. id. , a small hall , an antechamber , Cic. ad Q. Fr. 3, 1, 1 ; id. Att. 1, 10, 3 ; Inscr. Orell. 4509 ; Vulg. Ezech. 46, 21 bis; 46, 22; 46, 23.

ātrĭtas.opening: ater , blackness , Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 11 ; Paul. ex Fest. p. 28 Müll.; v. Müll. ad h. l.

Ăchĕrontĭa.opening: a small town of Apulia , near the frontiers of Lucania , situated on a hill , now Acerenza : celsa, Hor. C. 3, 4, 14 .

Ăchĕrontĭcus.opening: adj. , belonging to the Acheron or the Lower World : stagna, Prud. Cath. 5, 127 : libri, sacred books , written , according to tradition , by the Etruscan Tages , prob. relating to the Acherontian rites of the dead,…

Ăchĕruns.opening: v. Acheron ( , Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 2 ; cf. Non. 191, 24 ; poet. in Cic. Tusc. 1, 16, 37 ; the u for o, as in Enn. and Lucr. frundes for frondes, acc. Gr. Acherunta, Lucr. 4, 170 ; 6, 251 ); a form much used by…

Ăchĕrūsĭa.opening: Acheruns . Acherusia Palus, A lake in Epirus , through which the Acheron flows , Plin. 4, 1, 1 .— A lake in Campania , between Misenum and Cumae , now Lago di Fusaro , Plin. 3, 5, 9 .— A cave in Bithynia , from which…

Ăchĕrūsĭus.opening: (old writing Acherunsius), , adj. id. . Pertaining to the Acheron in Calabria : aqua, Liv. 8, 24 .— Pertaining to the Acheruns (Acheron), or the Lower World : templa, the Lower World , Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 21, 48…

Ăchillas.opening: the murderer of Pompey , Caes. B. C. 3, 104 ; 108 ; Luc. 8, 538 .

ăchillēa.opening: a plant , perhaps the same as achilleos , Plin. 26, 15, 90 .

Ăchillēĭs.opening: Achilles , a poem of Statius , of which only two books were finished, the Achilleid.

ăchillēos.opening: , = Ἀχίλλειος , sc. herba, a medicinal plant , said to have been discovered by Achilles , milfoil or yarrow , Plin. 25, 5, 19 ; cf. achillea.

Ăchilles.opening: , = Ἀχιλλεύς ( poet. , after the manner of the Gr. Nom. , Achilleus, trisyl., Inscr. Grut. 669, 6 .— Gen. Achillei, quadrisyl., Hor. C. 1, 15, 34 ; id. Epod. 17, 14 ; and Achilli, as Neocli, Lacydi from Neocles,…

Ăchillīdes.opening: patron. m. (more correct than Achilleides), = Ἀχιλλείδης , a descendant of Achilles , Ov. H. 8, 3 .

Ăchīvus.opening: ( gen. plur. Achivom, Verg. A. 11, 266 ), adj. fr. Achaeus, with the Digamma, Achaefos, Achifus, Achivus , Achaean , Grecian (v. Achaia): tellus, Ov. Pont. 1, 4, 33 : castra, id. H. 1, 21 .—Hence, , the Greeks , Cic.…

Ăcholla.opening: (also Achilla), a town in Africa , in the vicinity of Thapsus , now El-Aliah , Auct. B. Afr. 33.

ăchor.opening: , = ἀχώρ , the scab or scald on the head, Macer. de Ruta, 1, 12; Theod. Prisc. 1, 5 .

ăcĭa.opening: 1. acus , a thread for sewing , ῥάμμα , Titin. ap. Non. 3, 21 (R ib. Com. Rel. p. 115 ); Cels. 5, 26, 23 .

ăcĭcŭla.opening: id. , a small pin for a head-dress , Cod. Theod. 3, 16, 1 ; Inscr. Grut. 1004, 5 .

Ăcīdălĭa.opening: , = Ἀκιδαλία , an epithet of Venus , perhaps from the Fountain Acidalius, in Boeotia, where the Graces, daughters of Venus, used to bathe, Verg. A. 1, 720 Serv.—Hence, , , adj. , pertaining to Venus : ludit Acidalio…

ăcĭdĭtas.opening: acidus , sourness , acidity : stomachi, Marcell. Emp. 20.

ăcĭdŭlus.opening: adj. , dim. [acidus], a little sour , sourish , acidulous : sapor, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 54 : aqua, mineral water, id. 2, 103, 106, § 230 ; 31, 2, 5, § 9 ; so, fons, ib.

ăcĭdus.opening: adj. aceo , sour , tart , acid. Lit. : sapor, Plin. 15, 27, 32, § 106 ; sorba, Verg. G. 3, 380 : inula, Hor. S. 2, 2, 43 : lac, Plin. 28, 9, 36, § 135 : caseus, ib. 9, 34, § 132 : acidissumum acetum, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 49…

ăcĭēris.opening: , is acies , securis aerea, qua in sacrificiis utebantur sacerdotes, Paul. ex Fest. p. 10 Müll.

ăcĭēs.opening: v. 2. acer ( gen. acii and acie, like dii and die, facii and facie, fr. dies, facies, Cn. Mat. ap. Gell. 9, 14 ; Caes. B. G. 2, 23 ; Sall. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 208 , or Sall. Fragm. ed. Kritz. p. 118; cf. Prisc. p.…

Ăcīlĭānus.opening: adj. , pertaining to Acilius : annales, the annals of C. Acilius Glabrio, Liv. 25, 39 ; libri, id. 35, 14 .

Ăcīlĭus.opening: the name of several Romans , among whom was M' Acilius Glabrio , trib. pleb., by whom the severe law de pecuniis repetundis was introduced, Cic. Verr. 1, 9 and 17.—C. Acilius Glabrio, the historian , Cic. Off. 3, 32,…

ăcīnăcēs.opening: , = ἀκινάκης , the short sabre of the Persians , Medes , and Scythians , a scimitar , Hor. C. 1, 27, 5 ; Curt. 3, 3, 4 ; 4, 15, 17 al.

ăcĭnārĭus.opening: adj. acinus , pertaining to the grape : dolia, vessels for holding grapes, Varr. R. R. 1, 22, 4 .

ăcĭnātĭus.opening: adj. id. , prepared from grapes : vinum, made from dried grapes, Pall. 1, 6, 9 ; Dig. 33, 6, 9 .

ăcĭnos.opening: , = ἄκινος , a fragrant plant , perh. wild basil , Plin. 21, 27, 101, § 174 .

ăcĭnōsus.opening: adj. acinus , like or similar to grapes , Plin. 12, 13, 27, § 47 ; id. 21, 17, 68, § 109 .

ăcĭnus.grammar: i i ăcĭna, ae m. n. f.
ăcĭnus.opening: , and , , , partic. in plur. acina, orum (also , , Cat. 27, 4 ). A berry , esp. the grape , Col. 11, 2, 60 ; also: hederae sambucique, Plin. 15, 24, 29, § 100 sq. : cissanthemi, ib. 25, § 116 : ligustri, ib. 24, 74 :…

ăcĭpenser.opening: , and , (also aquip., not accipenser), , = ἀκκι^πησίος , a fish very highly esteemed in the age of the greatest luxury of the Romans , perh. the sturgeon , Cic. Tusc. 3, 18 ; id. Fin. 2, 8 ; Hor. S. 2, 2, 47 ; Ov. Hal.…

ăcisco.opening: , i. q., acesco, Garg. Mart. ap. Maj. Auct. Class. 3, p. 419.

ăciscŭlus.opening: perh. ascia, and so more prop. asciculus , a little adze , Isid. Gloss.— As a surname , Quint, 6, 3, 53. † , , acisculus , λατόμος ( stone-cutter ), Gloss.

ăcoenŏnŏētus.opening: , = ἀκοινονόητος , one who has not common-sense , Juv. 7, 218 : communi carens seusu, Schol. ad h. 1. (Herm. and Rib.; but Jahn and Mayor here read ἀκοινώνητος (in Greek letters); perh. not sharing , i. e. selfish ).

ăcoetis.opening: ἄκοιτις , a bed-fellow , a wife : Amphitryonis, Lucil. ap. Non. 26, 5 .

ăcŏnae.opening: , = ἀκόναι , pointed stones : nudae cautes, Plin. 27, 3, 3, § 10 .

ăcŏnīti.opening: adv. , = ἀκονιτί , without labor (lit. without dust , the figure taken from the athletae, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 51 ), Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 139 .

ăcŏnītum.opening: , = ἀκόνιτον , a poisonous plant , wolf's-bane , monk's-hood , aconite , Plin. 27, 2, 2 ; 6, 1, 1 fin. : aconiton, Ov. M. 7, 407 .—In plur. , Verg. G. 2, 152 ; Ov. M. 7, 419 ; Aus. Idyll. 12, 9, 11 ; Luc. 4, 322 . —For…

ăcontĭas.opening: , = ἀκοντίας . A quick-darting serpent , Amm. 22, 15, 27 .— In plur. , , , = ἀκοντίαι , meteors or shooting-stars with dartlike trains , Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 89 .

Ăcontĭus.opening: A lover of Cydippe , Ov. Her. 20, 239 , and 21, 229.— A mountain in Boeotia , Plin. 4, 7, 12 .

ăcontīzo.opening: v. n. , = ἀκοντίζω , lit., to shoot a dart; hence, intrans. of blood, to spout or gush forth , Veg. 1, 26 and 27.

Ăcontīzŏmĕnos.opening: , = Ἀκοντιζόμενος (struck with a dart), the title of a comedy of Naevius , see the fragment in, R ib. Com. Rel. p. 5 .

ăcŏpos.opening: , or , , , , = ἄκοπος (removing weariness, pain, etc.). A kind of stone , perh. crystalline quartz or spar , Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 143 .— , a plant useful in childbirth , also called anagyros , id. 27, 4, 13 .— (sc.…

ăcor.opening: aceo , a sour taste , sourness. Lit. , Col. 3, 21, 5 ; 7, 8, 1 ; Plin. 11, 41, 96 ; 18, 11, 26 ; of meat, Quint. 9, 3, 27 .— Fig. hortor ut jucundissimum genus vitae nonnullis interdum quasi acoribus condias, i. e.…

ăcorna.opening: , = ἄκορνα , a kind of thistle , Plin. 21, 16, 56, § 95 .

ăcŏrus.opening: , and , , , = ἄκορος and ἄκορον , an aromatic plant , conjectured by some to be our sweet-flag or calamus , Plin. 25, 13, 100, § 157 sq. ; 26, 5, 15, § 28 ; Cels. 3, 21 ; 2, 23 al. In the form , , , App. Herb. 6 .

Ăcrăgās.opening: Ἀκράγας ( acc. Gr. Acraganta, Ov. F. 4, 475 ), a mountain on the S. W. coast of Sicily , and a city upon it; the city was also called Agrigentum, now Girgenti , Verg. A. 3, 703 ; Mel. 2, 7, 16 ; cf. Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 89…

ăcrātŏphŏrum.opening: , = ἀκρατοφόρον , a vessel ( a pitcher or flask ) for holding unmixed wine , Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 5 ; Cic. Fin. 3, 4, 15 .

ăcrŏchordon.opening: , = ἀκροχορδών , a kind of wart , Cels. 5, 28, 14 .

ăcrŏpŏdĭum.opening: ἄκρος, extreme, and πούς, foot , the pedestal of a statue , Hyg. F. 88 .

ăcrōtērĭa.opening: , = ἀκρωτήρια , the projecting or extreme part of a thing. Of a harbor , Vitr. 5, 12 .— In architecture, the projecting parts of a pediment , serving as a support for figures or statues, Vitr. 3, 5, 12 sq. ; cf. Müll.…

ăcŭārĭus.opening: 1. acus , one who makes needles or pins , Inscr. Orell. 4139 .

ăcŭla.opening: dim. id. , a little needle , acc. to Cledon, p. 1896: frigit fricantem corpus acula (lect. dub.), Att. Rib. Trag. Rel. p. 195 .

ăcūlĕātus.opening: adj. aculeus , furnished with stings or prickles , thorny , prickly. Lit. , of animals and plants: animalia, Plin. 20, 22, 91 : bruchus, Vulg. Jer. 51, 27 : herbae, Plin. 24, 19, 119 : ictus, a puncture made by a sting,…

Ăcūlĕo.opening: a Roman cognomen in the gens Furia, Liv. 38, 55, 4 .—C. Aculeo, a famous lawyer , friend of L. Licinius Crassus , Cic. de Or. 1, 43, 191 ; 2, 1, 2 al.

ăcūlĕŏlus.opening: dim. aculeus , a little needle or pin : aculeolos in cochleare tulit, an old reading in Mart. 8, 71 , where now acu levius vix cochleare, is read.

ăcūlĕus.opening: acc. to Prisc. 618 P. dim. from 1. acus, with the gender changed, like diecula fr. dies, cf. Val. Prob. 1463 P. , a sting. Lit. Of animals: apis aculeum sine clamore ferre non possumus, Cic. Tusc. 2, 22 ; so Plin. 11,…

ăcūmĕn.opening: acuo , a point to prick or sting with; diff. fr. cacumen , which designates merely the summit or extremity of a thing, Doed. Syn. 2, 108. Lit. : tum clupei resonunt et ferri stridit acumen, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 838 P.…

ăcūmĭnārĭus.opening: adj. acumen , good for sharpening : mola, for sharpening weapons , Schol. ad Stat. Th. 3 .

ăcūmĭno.opening: v. a. id. , to make pointed , to sharpen , in verb finit. : contextum spinae acuminavit in caudam, Lact. Opif. 7, 7 .— Part. perf. : telum culicis, Plin. 11, 2, 1 : cornu lunae, id. 18, 35, 79 : corpus, id. 11, 24, 28 .

ăcŭo.opening: v. a. ( part. fut. acuturus, not used) [cf. 2. acer], to make sharp or pointed , to sharpen , whet. Lit. : ne stridorem quidem serrae audiunt, cum acuitur, Cic. Tusc. 1, 40 ; so, ferrum, Verg. A. 8, 386 ; Hor. C. 1, 2,…

ăcus.opening: 1. acus , a kind of sea-fish with a pointed snout , the hornpike or gar-pike (Gr. βελόνη ): acus sive belone unus piscium, etc., Plin. 9, 51, 76, § 166 : et satius tenues ducere credis acos, Mart. 10, 37, 6 ; cf. Plin.…

Ăcūsĭlas.opening: from Ἀκουσίλαος , an Argive historian , Cic. de Or. 2, 12, 53 .

ăcūtālis.opening: adj. acutus , pointed : terminus, Front. Col. p. 132 Goes.

ăcūtārus.opening: (for acutarius ), , adj. id. , that sharpens instruments : acutarus taber, Ins. ap. Henzen. 7216.

ăcūte.opening: adv. , v. acuo, P. a. fin.

ăcūtor.opening: acuo , one that sharpens , a sharpener , Not. Tir. p. 120 .

ăcūtŭle.opening: adv. , see the foll. art. fin.

ăcūtŭlus.opening: adj. dim. [acutus], somewhat pointed , acute , or subtile : conclusiones, * Cic. N. D. 3, 7, 18 : doctores, Gell. 17, 5 .— Adv. : , somewhat sharply , Aug. Conf. 3, 7 .

ăcўlos.opening: , = ἄκυλος , the acorn of the holm-oak (ilex), Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 19 (cf. Hom. Od. 10, 242).

ăcȳrŏlŏgĭa.opening: , = ἀκυρολογία , in rhetoric, an impropriety of speech; e. g.: sperare for timere, Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 419 (in pure Lat. improprium or impropria dictio is used instead of it: (quod proprietati est contrarium) id apud…

ădactĭo.opening: adigo , a forcing or bringing to : ad legitimam juris jurandi adactionem, to the taking of an oath, Liv. 22, 38 , where just before we find: milites jurejurando adacti.

ădactus.opening: adigo , a forcing or bringing to or together. —Hence, poet. , of the teeth, a biting , a bite : dentis adactus, Lucr. 5, 1330 .

ădaequātĭo.opening: adaequo , a making equal , an adjusting , adapting , Tert. ad Nat. 1, 1 ; Sol. 1 , where more correctly peraequatio.

ăd-aeque.opening: adv. , in like manner as , equally , so (most. ante- and post-class.; not in Cic.; and in Plautus always with the negatives nemo, numquam, neque, nullus, etc., by means of which the clause acquires a compar. signif.;…

ăd-aequo.grammar: āvi, ātum, 1 v. a. and n.
ăd-aequo.opening: v. a. and n. Act. To make equal to , to equalize , to level with; hence, In Cic. usually with cum (cf. aequare cum, Verg. A. 1, 193 ): qui cum virtute fortunam adaequavit, Cic. Arch. 10, 24 : quae ... admonet,…

ădaerātĭo.opening: adaero , a valuing , appraising , Cod. Th. 11, 20, 6; 11, 38, 13; 7, 4, 32.

ăd-aero.opening: v. ā. [aes], to estimate by money , to rate , appraise , value : in adaerandis reliquorum debitis non molestus, Amm. 31, 14 : ita ut nihil adaeretur, i. e. ita ut nihil in pecunia praestetur, Ep. Imp. Valeriani ap.…

ăd-aestŭo.opening: v. n. , to rush , to roar (with the idea of boiling up ): adaestuat amnis, Stat. Th. 5, 517 .

ăd-aggĕro.opening: v. a. (a double ad, as in adalligo), to heap up : cum ver adpetet, terram adaggerato bene, Cato, R. R. 94 : so, terram circa arborem, Col. 5, 11, 8 : terra Nilo adaggerata, brought down or deposited by the Nile , Plin.…

ădăgĭo.opening: , a rare form for adagium: adagione: proverbio, Gloss. Placid., Mai; Auct. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 31 Müll.; Aus. Monos. praef.

ădăgĭum.opening: prob. ad and aio, but acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 12 Müll., ad agendum apta, applicable to life, suitable for use , a proverb , an adage : vetus adagium est, Nihil cum fidibus graculo, Gell. 1, praef.

ăd-agnĭtĭo.opening: double ad, as in adaggero and adalligo , knowledge : Dei ignoti adagnitionem intentare, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 28 .

ăd-allĭgo.opening: v. a. (double ad, as in adaggero), to bind to , to fasten to , to attach : uncum (ad arborem), Plin. 17, 23, 35 , § 211: radices, id. 20, 21, 84, § 225 : vermiculos bracchio, id. 27, 10, 62, § 89 .

ădămantēus.opening: adj. adamas , of hard steel , iron , etc., or hard as these : catenae, adamantine, Manil. 1, 921 : nares (taurorum), Ov. M. 7, 104 .

ădămantĭnus.opening: adj. , = ἀδαμάντινος , hard as steel , etc., adamantine : saxa, Lucr. 2, 447 : duritia, Plin. 37, 11, 73 . —Hence poet. , extremely hard , inflexible , invincible : clavi, Hor. C. 3, 24, 5 : tunica, id. ib. 1, 6, 13 :…

ădămantis.opening: a certain magic herb , which cannot be bruised or crushed [ ἀ-δαμάω ], Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 162 ; App. Herb. 4 .

ădămas.opening: ( acc. Gr. adamanta, adamantas), = ἀδάμας (invincible), adamant , the hard est iron or steel; hence poet. , for any thing inflexible , firm , lasting , etc. (first used by Verg.): porta adversa ingens solidoque adamante…

ăd-ămātor.opening: a lover , Tert. Hab. Mul. 2 .—In the Gloss. Graec. a transl. of ἐρωτικός .

ăd-ambŭlo.opening: v. n. , to walk about , at , or near a thing (rare; used only before and after the class. per.): ad ostium, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 5, 8 .—Also with dat. : seni, App. M. 11, p. 261 ; so lateri, 3, 26.

ăd-ămo.opening: v. a. ad, intens. , to love truly , earnestly , deeply (in the whole class. per. mostly—in Cic. always— used only in the perf. and pluperf.; first in Col. 10, 199 , and Quint. 2, 5, 22 , in the pres. ): nihil erat…

ăd-amplĭo.opening: v. a. ad, den. increase , to widen , to enlarge , to increase : adampliemus pondus, Vulg. Ital. Amos, 8, 5, where St. Jerome has augeamus : aediculam vetustate corruptam adampliavit, Inscr. Grut. 128, 5 ; 884, 8 .

ăd-ăpĕrĭo.opening: v. a. ad, intens. , to open fully , to open , throw open (not in Cic.): adorti adapertas fores portae, Liv. 25, 30, 10 Drak. (cf. aperire forīs, Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 13 ); so Suet. Ner. 12 ; Curt. 9, 7, 24 ; Ov. Am. 1, 5, 3 ;…

ădăpertĭlis.opening: adj. adaperio , that may be opened : latus hoc adapertile tauri, Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 46 .

ădăpertĭo.opening: id. , an uncovering; hence, fig., a revealing , disclosure (late Lat.): legis, August. Quaest. 83, 61 .

ăd-apto.opening: v. a. , to fit , adjust , or adapt to a thing; with dat. only in part. pass. : galericulo capiti adaptato et annexo, Suet. Oth. 12 ; id. Claud. 33 .

ăd-ăquo.opening: v. a. aqua , to bring water to , to give to drink (postAug.), Vulg. Gen. 24, 46 ; 29, 10 .—Of plants: amygdalas, Plin. 17, 10, 11, § 64 : vites, Pall. 3, 33 .—* In pass. : adaquari (different from the foll.), to be…

ăd-ăquor.opening: v. dep. , to bring or procure water for one's self , io fetch water : nec sine periculo possent adaquari oppidani, Auct. B. G. 8, 41, where Dinter gives [ ad ] aquari; v. aquor.

ădarca.opening: , and , , , = ἀδάρκη, ἀδάρκης , a froth or efflorescence deposited on sedge , etc., forming a spongy growth , also called calamochnus; form adarca , Plin. 32, 10, 52, § 140 ; id. 16, 36, 66, § 167 ; 20, 22, 88, § 241 :…

ăd-āresco.opening: v. inch. [ad, intens. ], to dry up : ubi amurca adaruerit, vestimenta condito, Cato, R. R. 98 .

ădārĭārĭus.opening: adj. ad-ara , serving at the altar : MAGISTER ADARIARIVS, Burton, Inscr. p. 587.

ăd-ăro.opening: v. a. ad, intens. , to plough carefully : in an interpolation in Plin. 23, 1, § 2 .

ăd-aucto.opening: v. freq. [adaugeo], to augment much : rem summam et patriam nostram, Att. ap. Non. 75, 3 (R ib. Trag. Rel. p. 283 ).

ăd-auctor.opening: an augmenter , Tert. de Anim. 2 , where better auctor.

ădauctus.opening: adaugeo , an increasing , increase , growth : quaecunque vides hilaro grandescere adauctu, Lucr. 2, 1122 : lunae (opp. defectio), Sol. 23 fin.

ăd-augĕo.opening: v. a. , to make greater by adding to , to increase , augment. In gen.: timet, ne tua duritia adaucta sit, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 26 : haec maleficia aliis nefariis cumulant atque adaugent, Cic. Rosc. Am. 11 ; so id. Inv. 1,…

ăd-augesco.opening: v. inch. n. [ad, intens. ], to begin to increase or augment , to grow , to thrive : neque adaugescit quidquam neque deperit inde, Lucr. 2, 296 ; so also Cic. poet. in Div. 1, 7 fin.

ăd-bello.opening: to make war upon (late Lat.), Amm. 16, 9 .

ăd-ĕdo.opening: (less correctly, adessum), , v. a. (adest = adedit, Luc. 6, 265 ; cf. ĕdo), to begin to eat , to bite , to nibble at , to gnaw , etc.—As verb finite very rare, and mostly poet. ; not found in prose of Cic. Prop.: angues…

Ădelphi.opening: ( ), , , = ἀδελφοί , The Brothers , a comedy of Terence.

ădelphĭs.opening: ἀδελφή, sister; so called as resembling the caryotis, or because they hung two together from a branch , a kind of date , Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 45 .

ădemptĭo.opening: adimo , a taking away , a seizure : civitatis, Auct. Or. pro Dom. 30: bonorum, Tac. A. 4, 6 : provinciae, ib. 2, 76 .

ădemptor.opening: id. , one who takes away : vitae, Aug. in Joann. Tract. 116 .

ăd-ĕo.grammar: ĭī, and rarely īvi, ĭtum 4 v. n. and a.
ăd-ĕo.opening: (arch. adirier for adiri, Enn. Rib. Trag. p. 59 ), , v. n. and a. (acc. to Paul. ex Fest. should be accented a/deo; v. Fest. s. v. adeo, p. 19 Müll.; cf. the foll. word), to go to or approach a person or thing (syn.:…

ăd-ĕō^.opening: adv. cf. quoad and adhuc (acc. to Festus, it should be accented adéo, v. the preced. word ; but this distinction is merely a later invention of the grammarians; cf. Gell. 7, 7 ). In the ante-class. per., To designate…

Ădĕōna.opening: the tutelary goddess of new-comers , Aug. Civ. D. 4, 21 .

ădeps.opening: (in Plin. and Serv., ; in Cels., Quint., and Pallad., ; in Col. c.; cf. Prisc. 657 and 752 P.; Rudd. I. p. 34; Koffm. s. v.) [from ἄλειφα with interch. of d and l ], the soft fat or grease of animals , suet , lard (the…

ădeptĭo.opening: adipiscor , an obtaining , attainment : nos beatam vitam non depulsione mali, sed adeptione boni judicemus, Cic. Fin. 2, 13, 41 : bonorum (opp., malorum evitatio), Quint. 5, 10, 33 : alicujus commodi, Cic. Part. Or. 32,…

ădeptus.opening: , = adeptio, an obtaining : fidei, Paul. Nol. Ep. 32, 18 (in Cic. Fin. 3, 14, 48 , Henry Stephens reads: ad virtutis adeptum, but the true reading is habitum , Madv.).

ăd-ĕquĭto.opening: v. n. To ride to or toward a place, to gallop up to. —With ad : equites Ariovisti propius tumulum accedere et ad nostros adequitare, * Caes. B. G. 1, 46 .—With in : in primos ordines, Curt. 7, 4, 17 .—With the local…

ăd-erro.opening: v. n. , to wander to. — With dat. : scopulis, Stat. S. 2, 2, 120 .— Trop. : ululatus aderrat auribus, Stat. Th. 9, 178 .

ăd-esco.opening: v. a. , to feed or fatten : volantia adescata, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 11 .

ădesdum.opening: or (imper. from adsum with dum; cf.: agedum, manedum, etc., v. dum), come hither : Sosia, adesdum; paucis te volo, Ter. And. 1, 1, 2 .

ăd-ēsŭrĭo.opening: v. n. ad, intens. , to be very hungry : adesurivit et inhiavit acrius lupus, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 132 .

ăd-hăbĭto.opening: v. n. : adhabites, a false reading for adbites in Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 72 .

ăd-haerĕo.opening: v. n. , to cleave or stick to a thing. Lit. , of iron adhering to a magnet: unus ubi ex uno dependet, subter adhaerens, Lucr. 6, 914 ; cf. id. 3, 557 : tota adhaerens (lingua) crocodilis, cleaving to his palate, Plin.…

ăd-haeresco.opening: v. inch. [adhaereo], to cleave or stick to , to adhere , lit. and trop. (in the trop. sense almost exclusively belonging to Cic.). Lit. , constr. with ad , in , and abl. or ubi : tragula ad turrim, Caes. B. G. 5, 46 :…

ădhaese.opening: adv. adhaereo , hesitatingly , stammeringly : loqui, Gell. 5, 9 .

ădhaesĭo.opening: adhaereo , an adhering , adhesion : complexiones et copulationes et adhaesiones atomorum inter se, Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 19 , v. Madv. ad h. l.; Gloss. Placid. Clas. Auct. III. p. 427 Mai.

ădhaesus.opening: id. , an adhering , adherence (only in Lucr.): pulveris, Lucr. 3, 38 ; 4, 1242 : membrorum, id. 5, 842 : umoris, id. 6, 472 ; cf. Non. 73, 6 .

ăd-hālo.opening: v. a. , to breathe on : si patescentes (fungos) primo (serpens) adhalaverit, Plin. 22, 22, 46, § 95 .

ădhāmo.opening: v. a. hamus , to catch , secure : Qui serius honores adhamaverunt, vix admittuntur ad eos, Cic. ap. Non. 2, 5 , where Mercer. better reads adamaverunt.

ăd-hĭbĕo.opening: v. a. habeo , to hold toward or to , to turn , bring , add to; with ad , in , dat. or absol. In gen. Lit. : cur non adhibuisti, dum istaec loquereris, tympanum, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 38 : huc adhibete aurīs (ad ea) quae…

ădhĭbĭtĭo.opening: adhibeo (late Lat.). An admission (cf. adhibeo, II. C.): convivii, to a banquet, Gai. Inst. 1, 1 .— An employing , application (cf. ib. II. F.): cucurbitarum, Marc. Emp. 15 .

ăd-hinnĭo.grammar: īvi, or ĭi, ītum, 4 v. n.
ăd-hinnĭo.opening: v. n. , to neigh to or after. Lit. , constr. with dat. and acc. , also ad and in with acc. : fortis equus visae semper adhinnit equae, Ov. Rem. Am. 634 ; cf. id. A. A. 1, 208 ; Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 95 .—Hence, of lewd…

ăd-horrĕo.opening: , a false read. in Albinov. 1, 221, for inhorreo.

ădhortāmen.opening: adhortor , a means of exhortation , an exhortation : multa mihi apud vos adhortamina suppetunt, App. Flor. 4, 18, p. 359 .

ădhortātĭo.opening: id. , an exhortation , encouragement (class.): omissa nostra adhortatione veniamus ad eorum sermonem, * Cic. de Or. 2, 3, 11 : cum clamore comprobata adhortatio esset, Liv. 4, 38 ; 9, 13 ; Curt. 3, 11, 9 ; Plin. 8, 42,…

ădhortātīvus.opening: adj. adhortor , belonging to exhortation : modus, the mood of, Diom. I. p. 328 P. al.

ădhortātor.opening: id. , an exhorter , encourager , exciter : operis, Liv. 2, 58 .— Absol. , Liv. 7, 32 ; 9, 13 ; 32, 25 .

ădhortātus.opening: Part. of adhortor. * , , adhortor , an exhortation , persuasion : meo adhortatu, App. Mag. p. 338 .

ăd-hortor.opening: v. dep. , to encourage , urge , exhort one to a thing, constr. with ad , in , de , or absol. : nam me meae vitae consuetudo ad C. Rabirium defendendum est adhortata, Cic. Rab. Perd. 1 : ne posset aliquando ad bellum…

ăd-hospĭto.opening: v. a. , to entertain as guest. —Only trop.: Martem atque Concordiam multis immolationibus sibi adhospitavere, to propitiate, Dict. Cret. 1, 15 fin.

ăd-huc.opening: adv. Prop., of place, to this place , hitherto , thus far (designating the limit, inclusive of the whole space traversed: hence often joined with usque; cf. ad, A. 1. B.): conveniunt adhuc utriusque verba, thus far, to…

ădhūcĭne.opening: = adhuc ne, adv. interrog. , still? yet? App. M. 9, p. 218 , where some read adhucne.

Ădĭăbēna.opening: , or , , , = Ἀδιαβηνή , a region in the northern part of ancient Assyria , now Botan , Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 66 ; Amm. 23, 6, 20 al. — Hence, Derivv. , , adj. , pertaining thereto : Monobazus, Tac. A. 15, 14 ; so ib. 1 :…

ădĭantum.opening: , = ἀδίαντον , the plant maiden-hair , Plin. 22, 21, 30, § 62 (pure Lat.: capillus Veneris or capillaris herba, App. H. 47 ; Cael. Aurel. Tard. 3, 5).

ădĭăphŏros.opening: , = ἀδιάφορος , indifferent : nec dolere adiaphoron esse, Varr. ap. Non. 82, 14 (better here written as Greek; cf. Cic. Fin. 3, 16, 53 ).

Ădĭătŏrix.opening: king of the Comani , taken prisoner by Augustus at Actium , Cic. Fam. 2, 12, 2 .

ădĭbĭlis.opening: 1. adeo , accessible (late Lat.): terra, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 11, 18 .

ăd-ĭgo.opening: v. a. ago (adaxint = adegerint, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 11 ; Non. 75, 5 ; cf. adaxi for adegi), to drive , bring , or take a person or thing to a place (syn.: appello, adduco, affero).—Constr. usu. with ad , but also with…

ăd-ĭmo.opening: v. a. emo (adempsit = ademerit, Plaut. Ep. 3, 2, 27 ), to take to one's self from a person or thing, to take away , take any thing from , to deprive of (syn.: demere, eximere, auterre, eripere). Of things: si ego…

ăd-implĕo.opening: v. a. , to fill up , to fill full (in the class. per., e. g. in Liv. 38, 7, 13 , and Plin. 11, 37, 52, § 140 , dub.). Lit. : Gangem decem fluminibus adimpleri, Aethic. Cosmogr. p. 709 ed. Gron.: quasi mare adimpleti…

ădimplētĭo.opening: adimpleo . A completing , completion : temporum, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 17 .— A fulfilling , fulfilment : novum (testamentum) veteris adimpletio est, Lact. 4, 20 .

ădimplētor.opening: adimpleo , he who fills (by inspiration), the inspirer : Filius Dei adimpletor prophetarum, Aug. de Temp. Serm. 144, 3 .

ăd-incresco.opening: v. n. , to increase , Vulg. Eccli. 23, 3 .

ăd-indo.opening: v. a. , to put in besides : subscudes iligneas adindito, Cato, R. R. 18, 9 .

ăd-inflo.opening: v. a. , to swell up : pennas, August. C. D. 19, 23 .

ăd-ingĕro.opening: v. a. , to bring to in addition , to heap on : satiram in aliquem, Sisenn. ap. Serv. 2 .

ăd-inquīro.opening: v. a. , to investigate or inquire into further : aliquid, Jul. Val. 1, 49 Mai.

ăd-invĕnĭo.opening: v. a. ad, intens. , to find out , to devise , Vulg. Exod. 35, 33 ; Dig. 48, 19, 28 ; cf. also Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 603 : lapicaedinae adinventae sunt, Labi Ins.: si quis ainventus (for adinventus ) fuerit hoc fecisse,…

ădinventĭo.opening: adinvenio , an invention , Vulg. Judic. 2, 19 ; Isa. 3, 8 al.

ădinventor.opening: id. , an inventor; transl. of ἐφευρετής , Cyprian. Ep. 68, 10.

ădinventum.opening: id. , an invention , Tert. adv. Gnost. 1 .

ăd-invĭcem.opening: adv. , a strengthened form of invicem (q. v.), Aug. de Trin. 7 .

ăd-involvo.opening: v. a. , read by Alschefski in Liv. 1, 21 , manu ad digitos usque adinvolutā, but Weissenb. still reads involutā.

ădĭpālis.opening: adj. adeps , of or with fat , greasy : unguen, Arn. 3, p. 115 .

ădĭpātus.opening: adj. adeps , filled or supplied with fat , fatty , greasy. Lit. : puls, Lucil. ap. Charis. 73 and 74 P.; hence, absol. : (sc. edulium), i, pastry prepared with fat (cf. Charis. l. c.): livida materno fervent adipata…

ădĭpĕus.opening: adj. id. , of fat : tori, Hier. Ep. 147, 8 .

ăd-ĭpiscor.opening: v. dep. apiscor , to arrive at , to reach. Lit. : occepi sequi; vix adipiscendi potestas fuit, Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 13 .—Hence also with acc. , to reach , to overtake : fugientes Gallos Macedones adepti ceciderunt, Liv. 44,…

ădipsathĕon.opening: ἄδιψος - θεός, quenching the thirst of the gods , a low , thorny shrub , also called erysisceptrum or diacheton , Plin. 24, 13, 69, § 112 .

ădipsos.opening: , = ἄδιψος (quenching thirst). A species of date , Plin. 12, 22, 47, § 103 .— Liquorice , glycyrrhiza, Plin. 22, 9, 11, § 26 .

ădĭtĭālis.opening: adj. aditus , pertaining to entrance : cena, given by a magistrate when he entered upon his office, an inaugural feast, Varr. R. R. 3, 6, 6 ; Sen. Ep. 95, 41 ; 123, 4 ; Plin. 10, 20, 23, § 45 ; so, epulae, id. 29, 4,…

ădĭtĭcŭlus.opening: dim. id. , parvus aditus, Fest. p. 29 Müll.—The same in the fem. , , , Jul. Val. 3, 70 Mai.

ădĭtĭo.opening: 1. adeo . A going to , approach : quid tibi hanc aditio est? (i. e. aditio ad hanc, the verbal substantive with the case of the verb; v. Zumpt, § 681), why do you approach her? Plaut. Truc. 2, 7, 62 : praetoris, Dig.…

ădĭto.opening: v. freq. [id.], to go to or approach often : ad eum aditavere, Enn. ap. Diom. 336 P. (Trag. v. 433 ed. Vahl.); perh. also Col. 8, 3, 4 : aditet aviarius qui, etc. (instead of habitet ): si adites propius, os denasabit…

ădĭtus.opening: 1. adeo , a going to , approach , access. Lit. : quorum abitu aut aditu, Lucr. 1, 677 : urbes permultas uno aditu atque adventu esse captas, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 8 : quo neque sit ventis aditus, Verg. G. 4, 9 ; so id. A. 4,…

ăd-obrŭo.opening: v. a. , to cover up with earth , to bury : alte circumfodere et adobruere, Col. 4, 15, 3 ; so 2, 11, 12; 5, 5, 2; 11, 2, 54 al.

ădŏlātĭo.opening: , = adoratio, a read. in Tert. Apol. 25 fin.

ădŏlēfactus.opening: set on fire , kindled : ARBORES ADOLEFACTAE, fragm. of the Fratr. Arval., Grut. Inscr. p. 121 [1. adoleofacio].

ăd-ŏlĕo.opening: v. n. oleo , to give out or emit a smell or odor , to smell : unde hic, amabo, unguenta adolent? Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 19 (cf. aboleo).

ăd-ŏlesco.opening: (rare ui , Varr. ap. Prisc. 872 P.; adolēsse sync. for adolevisse, Ov. H. 6, 11 ), ultum, 3, v. inch. [1. adoleo], to grow up , to grow (of everything capable of increase in magnitude). In gen. Lit. , of men, animals,…

ădōmĭnātĭo.opening: a good or favorable omen , in Gloss. Gr. Lat.

Ădōneus.opening: (trisyl.). = Adonis, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 35 ; App. M. 2, p. 126 .— An epithet of Bacchus , Gr. Ἀδωνεύς, έως , Aus. Epigr. 30, 6 ; cf. id. ib. 28 .

Ădōnēus.opening: adj. , pertaining to Adonis: caedes, Aus. Mon. de Histt. 3 : lusus, Grut. Inscr. 1123, 7.

Ădōnĭa.opening: τὰ Ἀδώνια , the festival of Adonis. It returned annually in June, about the time of the summer solstice, and was celebrated (even in Rome; cf. Manso, Essays on Myth.) with alternate lamentations and exultations, on…

Ădōnis.opening: , = Ἄδωνις and Ἄδων ( nom. Adon, Venant. Carm. 7, 12 and 18; gen. Adonis, Plin. 19, 4, 19, § 49 ; dat. Adonidi, Cic. N. D. 3, 23 ; acc. Adonidem, Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 16: Adonim, Prop. 3, 5, 37 , acc. to Müller,…

ădōnĭum.opening: , = ἀδώνιον . Acc. to some a plant , a species of southernwood , bearing a flower of golden color or bloodred, as if from the blood of Adonis; acc. to others, a mode of cultivating flowers, as if Adonis horti , the…

ăd-ŏpĕrĭo.opening: v. a. , to cover up or over (not used before the Aug. per., and gen. in the part. perf. pass. ): capite adoperto, Liv. 1, 26 ; id. Epit. 89 , and Suet. Ner. 48 : purpureo adopertus amictu, Verg. A. 3, 405 : tempora…

ădŏpertē.opening: adv. adoperio , covertly , in a dark , mysterious manner : denuntiare, Mart. Cap. 8, p. 303 .

ădŏpertum.opening: id. , that which is mysterious , a mystery , App. M. 2 .

ăd-ŏpīnor.opening: v. dep. , to think , suppose , or conjecture further ( = opinando adicio): adopinamur de signis maxima parvis, Lucr. 4, 816 .

ădoptātīcĭus.opening: (not ), , adj. adopto , adopted , received in the place of a child; only in Plaut., Poen. 5, 2, 85: Demarcho item ipse fuit adoptaticius, ib. 100 . —Acc. to Festus, it signifies the son of one who is adopted : ex…

ădoptātĭo.opening: id.; access. form of adoptio, by which it was supplanted after the class. per. , an adopting , receiving as a child , υἱοθεσία : quid propagatio nominis, quid adoptationes filiorum, Cic. Tusc. 1, 14, 31 : adoptatio…

ădoptātor.opening: id. , one that adopts another , an adopter , Gell. 5, 19 ; Dig. 37, 9, 1, § 12 med.

ădoptĭo.opening: v. adoptatio , a taking or receiving of one in the place of a child (also of a grandchild , Dig. 1, 7, 10 ), an adopting , adoption (properly of one still under paternal authority, in patria potestate; on the contr.,…

ădoptīvus.opening: adj. adopto , pertaining to adoption , made or acquired by adoption , adoptive : filius, an adopted son : P. Scipio, Fragm. ap. Gell. 5, 19 (opp. naturalis, a son by birth): filiorum neque naturalem Drusum neque…

ăd-opto.opening: v. a. , to take to one's self by wish , choice (optando); to choose , select. In gen.: sociam te mihi adopto ad meam salutem, Plaut. Cist. 4, 2, 78 : qui manstutorem me adoptavit bonis, who has chosen me as a guardian…

ădor.opening: cf. 1. edo, ἔδομαι, Engl. to eat, Goth. ita, Sanscr. admi; and Ang.-Sax. ata = Engl. oat, and Sanscr. annam (for adnam) = food, corn , a kind of grain , spelt , Triticum spelta, Linn. (acc. to Paul. ex Fest.: Ador…

ădōrābĭlis.opening: adj. adoro , worthy of adoration , adorable : beneficium deae, App. M. 11, p. 265 .

ădōrātĭo.opening: id. , worship , adoration , προσκύνησις (rare; not in Liv. 30, 16, 5 , where the correct read. is adulationi, Weissenb.): propitiare deos adoratione, Plin. 29, 4, 20, § 67 .—In plur. , App. M. 4, p. 155 .

ădōrātor.opening: id. , one who adores , a worshipper , Tert. de Spec. 8 ; Vulg. Joh. 4, 23 .

ăd-ordĭno.opening: v. a. , to set in order , to arrange : patellam, Apic. 4, 2 .

ădōrĕa.opening: , and , , see the foll. art., II. A. and B.

ădōrĕus.opening: adj. ador , pertaining to spelt , consisting of spelt. Adj. : far adoreum = ador, Cato, R. R. 83 ; Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 4 ; Col. 11, 2, 74 sq. : semen, Cato, R. R. 34 ; Col. 2, 6, 1 : liba, Verg. A. 7, 109 : bellaria,…

ăd-ŏrĭo.opening: v. a. , the act. form of adorior, to attack , to assail : tunc ipsos adoriant, Naev. ap. Prisc. p. 801 P. (Trag. Rel. p. 8 Rib.).—Hence also pass. adortus, Aur. Fragm. Naev. ap. Prisc. p. 791 P.; and, acc. to some,…

ăd-ŏrĭor.opening: v. dep. ( part. adorsus, Gell. 9, 2, 10 ; see the passage at the end of this art.; the second and third pers. of the pres. ind. , acc. to the fourth conj.: adorīris, adorītur; forms analogous to orĕris, orĭtur, of the…

ădōrĭōsus.opening: adj. , in the Gloss. Gr. Lat. as translation of ἔνδοξος , that has often obtained the adorea, celebrated.

ăd-orno.opening: v. a. , to prepare a thing for some definite object, to get ready , to furnish , provide , fit out , equip , κοσμέω . In gen. (class.; esp. freq. in Plaut. and Cic.): quin tu mihi adornas ad fugam viaticum, Plaut. Ep.…

ăd-ōro.opening: v. a. In the earliest per., to speak to or accost one, to address; hence, also, to treat of or negotiate a matter with one : adorare veteribus est alloqui, Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 677 : immo cum gemitu populum sic adorat,…

ăd-oscŭlor.opening: v. dep. , to give a kiss to , to kiss : manus, Dict. Cret. 2, 51 .

ădūlābĭlis.opening: (not ), , adj. adulor , suited to flatter , flattering , adulatory : sermo, Amm. 14, 11 : sententia, id. 31, 12 ; cf. Non. 155, 30 .

ădūlātĭo.opening: adulor , a fawning , like that of a dog (adulatio est blandimentum proprie canum, quod et ad homines tractum consuetudine est, Non. 17, 4 ).—In the post-Aug. historians, esp. in Tac., very freq. for a servile respect…

ădūlātor.opening: id. , a low , cringing flatterer , a sycophant (homo fallax et levis, ad voluptatem facit ac dicit omnia, nihil ad veritatem, Cic. Lael. 25, 91 ; cf. id. ib. 25, 93 ): nolo esse laudator, ne videar adulator, Auct. Her.…

ădūlātōrĭus.opening: adj. adulator , flattering , adulatory (rare): dedecus, Tac. A. 6, 32 fin.—Adv. : , flatteringly , fawningly : agere rem, August. Ep. 148 .

ădūlātrix.opening: id. , a female flatterer : adulatrices exterae gentes, Treb. Poll. Claud. 3 ; so tert. Anim. 51.

ădŭlescens.opening: (only in the verb and part. proper ), entis ( gen. plur. usu. adulescentium, e. g. Cic. Tusc. 5, 27 al. : adulescentum, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 130 ). P. a. , growing up , not yet come to full growth , young : eodem ut jure…

ădŭlescentĭa.opening: (not ), ae. adulescens , the age of the adulescens, the time between the age of the puer and juvenis, i. e. from the 15th to the 30th year , the time of youth , youth , = ἐφηβία, ἡλικία (cf. adulescens): quid enim?…

ădŭlescentĭor.opening: (not ), , v. dep. id. , to behave like an adulescens: tu adhuc adulescentiaris, Varr. ap. Non. 71, 30 .

ădŭlescentŭla.opening: (not ), , dim. id. , a very young maiden; also as a term of endearment for an adult: salveto, adulescentula, good morrow, my child, Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 3 ; Ter. And. 1, 1, 91 : adulescentula speciosa, Vulg. 3 Reg. 1, 3 :…

ădŭlescentŭlus.opening: (not ), , dim. id. , a very young man , = νεανίσκος (when 27 years old, Cicero calls himself adulescentulus, Or. 30; cf. Gell. 15, 28 , and Quint. 12, 6 . So Sall. C. 49 calls Cæsar adulescentulus, although he was then…

ădŭlescentūrĭō.opening: (not ), , v. n. id. , to behave like an adulescens: incipio adulescenturire et nescio quid nuga rum facere, Laber. ap. Non. 74 15 Com Rel. p. 299 Rib.).

ădūlo.opening: v. a. (a rare form for adulor; hence Prisc. 791 P. ranks this form, as an exception, among the other active forms of the deponents, adipiscor, admiror, auxilior, etc.; cf. Don. p. 1756 P. and Ars Consent. p. 2054 P.),…

ădūlor.opening: v. dep. acc. to Lobeck, the -ulo, -ulor is connected with ἴλλειν (cf. εἰλύω, ἐλύω, and volvo), and thus denoted orig. the wagging of the tail and fawning of brutes; Fest. p. 21 Müll., thought adulor was a form of…

ăd-ulter.opening: , and , , alter, acc. to Fest.: adulter et adultera dicuntur, quia et ille ad alteram et haec ad alterum se conferunt, p. 22 Müll. , orig. one who approaches another ( from unlawful or criminal love ), an adulterer or…

ădulter.opening: adj. (Rudd. I. p. 51, n. 36), for adulterinus, adulterous , unchaste : crines, finely-curled hair, like that of a full-dressed paramour, Hor. C. 1, 15, 19 : mens, that thinks only of illicit love, Ov. Am. 3, 4, 5 :…

ădultĕrātĭo.opening: adultero , an adulteration , sophistication : croci, Plin. 21, 6, 17, § 32 ; so prooem. 1, 2.

ădultĕrātor.opening: id. , a counterfeiter : monetae, Cod. Th. 11, 21, 1; Dig. 48, 19, 16 fin.

ădultĕrātrix.opening: , = adultera, Gloss. Gr. Lat. as trans. of μοιχαλίς .

ădultĕrīnus.opening: adj. adulter . Adulterous : liberi adulterino sanguinen nati, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 14 ; and of animals, not full-blooded : pullus adulterinus et degener, id. 10, 3, 3, § 10 .—But oftener, That has assumed the nature of…

ădultĕrĭo.opening: , ōnis. A word formed by Laberius = adulter, acc. to Non. 70, 5 ; or adulterium, acc. to Gell. 16, 7 , the latter of whom censures this form.

ădultĕrĭum.opening: adulter . Adultery : Adulterium est cum aliena uxore coire, Quint. 7, 3, 10 : qui in adulterio deprehenditur, Cic. de Or. 2, 68, 275 : mulierem in adulterio deprehensam, Vulg. Joan. 8, 3 : cum aliqua facere, Cat. 67, 36…

ădultĕro.grammar: āvi, ātum, 1 v. n. and a.
ădultĕro.opening: v. n. and a. [id.], to commit adultery , to pollute , defile. Lit. , absol. or with acc. : latrocinari, fraudare, adulterare, Cic. Off. 1, 35 : jus esset latrocinari: jus adulterare: jus testamenta falsa supponere, id.…

ădumbrātim.opening: adv. adumbro , sketched in shadow , à la silhouette, in general or in outline (opp. adamussim): quasi adumbratim paulum simulata videntur, as it were covered with shadows, dimly resembling, Lucr. 4, 363 .

ădumbrātĭo.opening: id. , a sketch in shadow , à la silhouette, a perspective sketch or draft (cf. adumbro). Lit. : scenographia est frontis et laterum abscedentium adumbratio, Vitr. 1, 2 .— Fig., a sketch , outline : nulla est laus…

ăd-umbro.opening: v. a. , to bring a shadow over a thing , to cast a shadow on , to shade or overshadow by something. In gen. Lit. , constr.: aliquid aliqua re (so only in later authors): palmeis tegetibus vineas, Col. 5, 5 : adumbrantur…

ădūnātĭo.opening: (like the verb aduno, only in later authors), a making into one , a uniting , a union , ἕνωσις , Cyp. Ep. 57 (60 Oxon.), 61 (62 ib.); Cassiod. Ep. 4, 33 and 36.

ăduncĭtas.opening: aduncus , the curvature of a point inwards , hookedness , aduncity : rostrorum, * Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 122 ; so, rostri, Plin. 8, 27, 41, § 97 ; 10, 71, 91, § 196 .

ăd-uncus.opening: adj. , bent in the manner of a hook , hooked : nasus, a hooked or aquiline nose , * Ter. Heaut. 5, 5, 18 (on the contr. reduncus nasus, a snub or turned-up nose): serrula adunca ex omni parte dentium et tortuosa, Cic.…

ăd-ūno.opening: v. a. , to make one , to unite (in Just. several times, elsewhere rare, except in the Chr. fathers): cum adunata omnis classis esset, Just. 2, 12 ; so 7, 1; 15, 4; Pall. 3, 29 ; 4, 10 ; Lact. Opif. D. 17 al. (Non. reads…

ăd-urgĕo.opening: v. a. , to press to or close to , press against. — Lit. : dens digito adurgendus, Cels. 7, 12, 1 .— Poet. : (aliquem) remis volantem, i. e. to pursue closely, Hor. C. 1, 37, 17 .

ăd-ūro.opening: v. a. , to set fire to , to kindle , to set in a flame , to burn , singe , scorch (cf. accendo), etc. Lit. , of food: hoc adustum est, * Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 71 ; so Hor. S. 2, 8, 68 ; 90 : splendor quicunque est acer, adurit…

ăd-usque.opening: (like abusque for usque ab); hence, Prep. with acc. , to , quite or even to , all the way to , as far as (rare, not used in Cic., and for the most part only in the poets of the Aug. per. ( metri gratiā ) and their…

ădustĭo.opening: aduro . A kindling , burning; a burn (concrete only in Pliny): ulcera frigore aut adustione facta, Plin. 32, 4, 14, § 34 : adustiones sanat (lactuca), id. 20, 7, 26, § 61 .—Also of plants, e. g. vines, a rubbing ,…

ăd-ūtor.opening: , a false reading in Cato, R. R. 76, 4 , instead of abusus.

ădўnămon.opening: vīnum = ἀδύνατος οἶνος , weakened wine (half wine and half water): ex ipso vino quod vocant adynamon, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 100 .

ădўtum.opening: , = ἄδυτον (not to be entered), the innermost part of a temple , the sanctuary , which none but priests could enter , and from which oracles were delivered. Lit. : in occultis ac remotis templi, quae Graeci ἄδυτα…

ăēdon.opening: ( ), , , = ἀηδών , the nightingale : tristis aëdon, Sen. Agam. 670 ; so Petr. Sat. 131 ; Calp. Ecl. 6, 8 .

ăēdŏnĭus.opening: adj. (pentasyl.) [aëdon], pertaining to the nightingale : vox, Auct. Pan. ad Pison. 257; Lact. Phoenic. 47 .

Ăëllō.opening: , = Ἀελλώ . The name of a harpy (from ἄελλα , tempest, because she came like it upon her prey): ales Aëllo, Ov. M. 13, 710 .— The name of a swiftrunning dog , Ov. M. 3, 219 .

ăēnĕŏlus.opening: adj. dim. [aeneus], made of bronze : aeneoli piscatores, little figures of fishermen in bronze, Petr. S. 13 ; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 28 Müll.

ăēnĭpes.opening: or , , adj. aeneus-pes , that has feet of bronze , bronzefooted , χαλκόπους : boves, Ov. H. 6, 32 : equi, Prud. adv. Symm. 1, 531 .

Ăēnŏbarbus.opening: (earlier, ), , aeneus, II., and barba. Red-beard , a family name of the Domitian gens, Suet. Ner. 1 Oud.; Inscr. Orell. 3793 .

ăēnus.opening: (trisyl.; less freq. ), , adj. aes , of copper or bronze (only poet. for aheneus; yet Hor. uses the latter oftener than the former). Lit. : signa, the bronze images of the gods , Lucr 1, 316: ahënis in scaphiis, id. 6,…

Ăgămēdēs.opening: , = Ἀγαμήδης , a brother of Trophonius , with whom he built the temple to the Delphic Apollo , Cic. Tusc. 1, 47, 114 .

Ăgămemnon.opening: ( nom. Agamemno, Enn. ap. Cic. Att. 13, 47 ; Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 17 ; Stat. Achill. 1, 553 ), = Ἀγαμέμνων , king of Mycenœ , son of Atreus and of Aërope , brother of Menelaüs , husband of Clytœmnestra , father of Orestes ,…

ăgămus.opening: adj. , = ἄγαμος , unmarried , Hier. adv. Jovian. 1 and 15.

Ăgănippē.opening: , = Ἀγανίππη . A fountain in Bœotia , on Mount Helicon , sacred to the Muses , and giving poetical inspiration : Aonie Aganippe, Verg. E. 10, 12 ; Claud. Ep. ad Ser. 61 .—Hence, , , adj. , = Ἀγανίππειος , of or…

ăgăpē.opening: , = ἀγάπη (love). Christian love or charity , Tert. ad Martyr. 2 .— The love-feast of the early Christians , Tert. Apol. 39 fin.

ăgărĭcum.opening: , = Ἀγαρικόν , larch fungus , tinder fungus , Plin. 25, 9, 57, § 103 ; 26, 8, 48 .

ăgāso.opening: ago, as Sanscr. agas from ag; v. ago , a driver , but esp. one who drives and takes care of horses , a hostler , groom , Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 11 : duo equi cum agasonibus, Liv. 43, 5 : agasonem cum equo, Plin. 35, 11, 40…

Ăgăthō^cles.opening: , = Ἀγαθοκλῆς . A king of Sicily , son of a potter , celebrated for his war with the Carthaginians for the possession of the island; cf. Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 55 ; Val. Max. 7, 4, 1 ext.; and esp. Just. 22, 1 sq. —Hence, , ,…

ăgăthŏdaemon.opening: , = ἀγαθοδαίμων (good genius), a kind of serpent in Egypt to which healing power was ascribed , Coluber Aesculapii, Linn.; Lampr. Heliog. 28 .

Ăgăthyrna.opening: , = Ἀγάθυρνον , Strab., a town on the northern coast of Sicily , between Tyndaris and Calacta , Liv. 26, 40 ; 27, 12 ; Sil. 14, 259 ; Mel. 2, 5 .

Ăgăthyrsi.opening: , = Ἀγάθυρσοι , a Scythian people ( in what is now Transylvania , and the Bannat of Temeswar ) who commonly painted their faces and limbs; hence Vergil: picti Agathyrsi, A. 4, 146; cf. Plin. 4, 12, 26 ; and Mel. 2, 1 .

Ăgāvē.opening: or , , , = Ἀγαύη . A daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia , wife of Echion , king of Thebes , who tore in pieces with her own hands her son Pentheus , because he cast contempt upon the orgies of Bacchus , Ov. M. 3, 725 ;…

Ăgĕlastus.opening: , = ἀγέλαστος (not laughing), a surname of M. Crassus , grandfather of the triumvir of the same name , Plin. 7, 19, 18, § 79 ; cf. Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 5, 30, 92 , and Tusc. 3, 15, 31.

ăgellŭlus.opening: a double dim. of ager; cf. asellulus , a very small field , Symm. Ep. 2, 30 .

ăgellus.opening: dim. ager , a small piece of ground , a little field; Agelli est hic sub urbe paulum quod locitas foras, Ter. Ad. 5, 8, 26 : agellus non sane major jugero uno, Varr. R. R. 3, 16 : minora dii neglegunt, neque agellos…

ăgēmă.opening: , = ἄγημα , in the Macedonian army, a corps or division of soldiers : addita his ala mille ferme equitum: agema eam vocabant, Liv. 37, 40 ; 42, 51 ; so id. 42, 58 ; Curt. 4, 13, 26 .

Ăgendĭcum.opening: a town in Gallia Lugdunensis , acc. to the Tabul. Peuting. Agedicum, now Sens , Caes. B. G. 6, 44 ; 7, 10 .

Ăgēnor.opening: , = Ἀγήνωρ , a son of Belus , king of Phœnicia , father of Cadmus and Europa , and ancestor of Dido; hence, poet. , Agenoris urbs, i. e. Carthage , Verg. A. 1, 338 .—Agenore natus, i. e. Cadmus , Ov. M. 3, 51 ; 97 ; 257…

ăger.opening: ἀγρός; Germ. Acker, Eng. acre, Sanscr. agras = surface, floor; Grimm conjectured that it was connected with ago, ἄγω, a pecore agendo, and this was the ancient view; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 34 Müll., and Don. ad Ter. Ad.…

ăgērăton.opening: , = ἀγήρατον (not growing old), a plant that does not readily wither , perhaps Achillea Ageraton, Linn.; Plin. 27, 4, 4, § 13 .— , , , a designation of one of the Æons of Valentinus , Tert. adv. Val. 8 .

Ăgēsĭlāüs.opening: , = Ἀγησίλαος . One of the most valiant of the Spartan kings , who conquered the Persian satrap Tissaphernes , and the Athenians and Boeotians at Coronea. Plutarch and also Nepos wrote his life.—* An epithet of Pluto…

ăgĕsīs.opening: , i. e. age sis, v. ago, II. 12.

ăgĭlĭtas.opening: agilis , the condition of agilis, mobility , nimbleness , activity , quickness , fleetness , agility. Lit. : navium, Liv. 26, 51 : rotarum, Curt. 4, 6 : cursus et agilitas alicujus, mobility, Quint. 11, 3, 180 . — Trop.…

ăgīna.opening: ago , the opening in the upper part of a balance , in which the tongue moves (agitur), Paul. ex Fest. p. 10 Müll.; cf. also Tert. adv. Herm. 41 ; Pudic. 9.— Hence, † , Paul. ex Fest. p. 10 Müll.

ăgĭpēs.opening: ago-pes , in Lucilius = pedarius senator, a senator who silently passes over to him for or with whom he intends to vote , Fest. s. v. pedarium, p. 210 Müll.; agipes ut vocem mittere coepit, Lucil. p. 145 Müll.

ăgĭtābĭlis.opening: adj. agito , that can be easily moved , easily movable (as an epitheton ornans of the air), light : aër, Ov. M. 1, 75 .

ăgĭtātĭo.opening: id. , the state of being in motion , motion , movement , agitation (in good class. prose). Lit. : agitationes fluctuum, Cic. Mur. 17 : agitatio et motus linguae, id. N. D. 2, 54 : lecticae, Liv. 27, 29 : agitatione…

ăgĭtātor.opening: id. , pr. he that puts a thing in motion; used exclusively of those who drive animals (asses, horses, etc.), a driver (cf. agaso): agitator aselli, poet. for a peasant , Verg. G. 1, 273 : equorum Achillis, i. e. the…

ăgĭtātrix.opening: agitator , she that puts a thing in motion (late Lat.): silvarum agitatrix Diana, i. e. huntress, Arn. 4, p. 141 . — Trop. , App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 6, 15 Elm.

ăgĭtātus.opening: agito , a state of motion , a being in motion , movement , agitation (only ante- and post-class.). Lit. , Varr. L. L. 5, § 12 Müll. dub. (Müll. reads: ubi id agitatur); id. ib. 6 , § 41 Müll.: anima corpori praestat…

ăgĭto.opening: v. freq. a. ago , as if the supine were agitu; cf.: quaero quaerito. Lit. , to put a thing in motion , to drive or impel (mostly poet. , or in more elevated prose; from poetry it passed, after the Aug. per., into common…

ăgo.opening: v. a. (axim = egerim, Pac. ap. Non. 505, 22 ; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. axitiosi, p. 3 Müll.; axit = egerit, Paul. Diac. 3, 3 ; AGIER = agi, Cic. Off. 3, 15 ; agentūm = agentium, Vulc. Gall. Av. Cass. 4, 6 ) [cf. ἄγω ;…

ăgōgae.opening: , = ἀγωγαί (or - οί ) a conduit or aqueduct), in mines, channels or passages for drawing off water , Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 76 , v. Sillig ad h. l.

ăgŏlum.opening: from ago, as cingulum from cingo , a shepherd's staff or crook : pastorale baculum, quo pecudes aguntur , Paul. ex Fest. p. 29 Müll.

ăgōn.opening: , = ἀγών , gen. ῶνος a contest or combat in the public games : gymnicus, Plin. Ep. 4, 22 : non esse restituendum Viennensibus agona, id. ib. 4, 22 fin. : musicus, Suet. Ner. 22 ; so id. ib. 23 .—Hence, prov.: nunc demum…

Ăgōnālĭa.opening: (like Saturnalia, Parentalia, etc.), , a festival in honor of Janus , celebrated in Rome on the 9 th of Jan. (V. Id. Jan.) and 21 st of May (XII. Kal. Jun.).—Different derivations of the word were given by the ancients,…

Ăgōnālis.opening: adj. , pertaining to the Agonalia (cf. preced. art.): dies Agonales, per quos rex in regiā arietem immolat; dicti ab Agone (the leader, the chief), eo quod interrogatur a principe civitatis et princeps gregis immolatur,…

Ăgōnensis.opening: adj. Porta Agonensis, one of the gates of Rome , also called Collina and Quirinalis, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. Agonium, p. 10 Müll.; cf. Smith's Dict. Antiq. — Salii Agonenses, the priests who officiated upon the Quirinalis…

ăgōnĭa.opening: A victim , v. agonium.— = Agonalia, Ov. F. 5, 721 ; cf. agonium.

ăgōnistă.opening: , = ἀγωνιστής , a combatant for a prize , Aug. Serm. 343 fin. † † , , , = ἀγωνιστάρχης , the superintendent of public games , Inscr. Grut. 38, 5 .

ăgōnĭum.opening: : dies appellabatur, quo rex (sacrificulus) hostiam immolabat. Hostiam enim antiqui agoniam vocabant. Agonium etiam putabant deum dici praesidentem rebus agendis; Agonalia ejus festivitatem, sive quia agones dicebant…

ăgōnŏthĕtă.opening: and , , , = ἀγωνοθέτης , the superintendent of public games , Spart. Hadr. 13 ; Tert. Mart. 3 al.

ăgŏrānŏmus.opening: , = ἀγορανόμος (clerk of the market), a Grecian magistrate , who had the inspection of provisions , and their purchase and sale; the Aedilis plebis of the Romans, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 43 ; so id. Curc. 2, 3, 6 .

Ăgyīeus.opening: , = Ἀγυιεύς (trisyl.), ĕï or eos, an epithet of Apollo , as guardian deity of the streets ( ἀγυιαί ), since his statues stood in them: levis Agyieu, Hor. C. 4, 6, 27 .

Ăgylla.opening: a town in Etruria , called later Caere, now Cervetri , Verg. A. 8, 479 ; Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 51 .—Hence, , inhabitants of Agylla , Verg. A. 12, 281 .

Ăgȳrĭum.opening: a very old town in Sicily , not far from Enna , the birthplace of Diodorus Siculus , now S. Filippo d'Argiro , Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 28 .—Hence, , , Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 28 ; or , , inhabitants of Agyrium , Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91 .

ăhă.opening: interj. acc. to Prisc. 570 P., primitive of the preced., but more rare , aha! ah! haha! an exclamation. Of reproof or denial: aha, tace, Plaut. Truc. 4, 4, 36 ; id. Rud. 2, 4, 6 : aha, minime, id. Bacch. 1, 1, 54 .— Of…

Ăhāla.opening: a Roman family name , e. g. C. Servilius Ahala, who slew the turbulent Maelius, Cic. Cat. 1, 1, 3 ; id. Sen. 16, 56 .

ăīthăles.opening: , = ἀειθαλές (evergreen), a plant , also called Aizoon, houseleek , App. Herb. 123 .

ăīzōŏn.opening: , = ἀείζωον (ever-living), an evergreen plant. Majus, live-forever , houseleek : Sempervivum tectorum, Linn.; Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160 .— Minus or minusculum, stone-crop : Sedum album, Linn.; Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160 .

Ălăbanda.opening: and , , a city in the interior of Caria , distinguished for its wealth and luxury , founded by Alabandus , who was honored by the inhabitants as a deity; now Arab-Hissar; plur. form, Cic. N. D. 3, 15 ; 3, 19 ; Liv. 33,…

ălăbaster.opening: ( plur. also , ), = ἀλάβαστρος , plur. -ρα . A box or casket for perfumes , tapering to a point at the top , a box for unguents : alabaster plenus unguenti, * Cic. Ac. Post. ap. Non. 545, 15 : mulier habens alabastrum…

ălăbastrītes.opening: , = ἀλαβαστρίτης . A stone , composed of carbonate of lime (not of gypsum, like the modern alabaster), alabaster-stone; also called onyx and onychites, from which unguent and perfume boxes were made, Plin. 36, 8, 12, §…

Ălăbastron.opening: ( Ἀλαβαστρῶν πόλις , Ptol.), a city of Egypt in the Thebais , Plin. 5, 9, 11, § 61 .

ălăbēta.opening: , = ἀλαβής , a fish found in the Nile : Silurus anguillaris, Linn.; Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 51 .

ălăcer.opening: adj. (also in masc. alacris, Enn., v. below; Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 13 , and Verg. A. 5, 380 ; cf. Charis. p. 63 P.—In more ancient times, alacer ; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 685 , and 2. acer) [perh. akin to alere = to nourish,…

ălăcrĭtas.opening: alacer , the condition or quality of alacer, liveliness , ardor , briskness , alacrity , eagerness , promptness , joy , gladness : alacritas rei publicae defendendae, Cic. Phil. 4, 1 : mirā sum alacritate ad litigandum,…

Ălānus.opening: adj. , of or pertaining to the Alani , = Ἀλανοί , a very warlike Scythian nation upon the Tanais and Palus Mœotis : gens Alana, Claud. B. Get. 583 .— Subst. : , , , one of the Alani , Luc. 10, 454 .— Com. plur. : , ,…

ălăpa.opening: akin to -cello, to smite, as if calapa; cf. κόλαφος , a stroke or blow upon the cheek with the open hand , a box on the ear : ducere gravem alapam alicui, to give, Phaedr. 5, 3 : ministri eum alipis caedebant, Vulg.…

ălăpus.opening: alapa , a parasite , who submitted to the box on the ear for gold , Gloss. Isid.; cf. Barth. Advers. 19, 22.

Ălărīcus.opening: Alaric , a king of the Goths , Claud. B. Get. 431 .

Ălastor.opening: , = ἀλάστωρ (a tormentor). One of the companions of Sarpedon , king of Lycia , killed by Ulysses before Troy , Ov. M. 13, 257 .— Name of one of the four horses in the chariot of Pluto , Cland. R. Pros. 1, 284.

ălăternus.opening: perh. akin to Germ. Erle; Engl. alder , a shrub : Rhamnus Alaternus, Linn.; Col. 7, 6 ; Plin. 16, 26, 45, § 108 .

ălauda.opening: Celtic; lit. great songstress, from al, high, great, and aud, song; cf. the Fr. alouette; Breton. al' choueder; v. Diefenbach in Zeitschriften für vergl. Sprachf. IV. p. 391 . The lark , Plin. 11, 37, 44, § 121 .— , the…

ălausa.opening: Fr. alose , a small fish in the Moselle , the shad : Culpea alosa, Linn.; Aus. Mos. 127 .

ălāzōn.opening: , = ἀλαζών (boasting), a braggart , boaster , Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 8 .

Ălāzon.opening: a river in Albania , now Alasan , Plin. 6, 10, 11, § 29 ; Val. Fl. 6, 102 .

ălebrĭa.opening: alo , nourishing food , = bene alentia, Paul. ex Fest. p. 25 Müll.

ălectŏrĭus.opening: adj. , pertaining to a cock ( ἀλέκτωρ ): gemma, a gem found in the maw of a cock, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 144 .

ălectŏrŏlŏphŏs.opening: , = ἀλεκτορόλοφος , an herb good for a cough , cock's comb : Rhinanthus crista galli, Linn.; Plin. 27, 5, 23, § 40 .

Ălēĭus.opening: adj. , = Ἀλήϊος , of or pertaining to Ale in Lycia : Aleïi campi, where Bellerophon, having been thrown from Pegasus, and blinded by the lightning of Jupiter, wandered and perished, Hyg. Fab. 57 ; Ov. Ib. 259 : qui…

Ălĕmanni.opening: ( and ), , = Alle-Männer , the Alemanni , German tribes who (as their name indicates) formed a confederation on the Upper Rhine and Danube , from whom the Gauls transferred the name to the whole German nation; cf. Aur.…

Ălēmon.opening: ἀλήμων, a wanderer , a Greek; father of Myscelus , who built Crotona in Lower Italy , Ov. M. 15, 18 .

Ălĕmōna.opening: ( ), , alo , a tutelar goddess of the fœtus , Tert. Anim. 37 .

Ălēmŏnĭdēs.opening: patr. , the son of Alemon , i. e. Myscelus , who founded Crotona in Lower Italy , Ov. M. 15, 26 .

Ălĕrĭa.opening: , = Ἀλερία , the oldest town of the island Corsica , captured by L. Scipio: HEC. CEPIT. CORSICA(m). ALERIA(m) QVE. VRBE(m), the second epitaph of the Scipios in Grotef. 4, 298; cf. Wordsw. p. 160; Mannert. Ital. 2, 516…

ălesco.opening: v. inch. n. [alo], to grow up , increase (only ante-class.), Varr. R. R. 1, 44, 4 ; 2, 4, 19 : alescendi cacumen, * Lucr. 2, 1130 .

Ălĕsĭa.opening: , = Ἀλεσία , Diod. Sic., a city of the Mandubii in Celtic Gaul , now Alise in the Dép. de la Cōte d' Or , Caes. B. G. 7, 68 ; id. B. C. 3, 47 ; Vell. 2, 47 .—Also, , , , = Ἀλεξία Strabo, Flor. 2, 2 ; cf. Mannert Gall.…

Ălēthīa.opening: , = ἀλήθεια (truth), one of the Æons of Valentinus , Tert. Valent. 12 .

Ălētīnus.opening: an inhabitant of the town Aletium, in the land of the Hirpini , now Calitri (* acc. to others, Lecce ), Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105 .

Ălētrĭum.opening: a town in Latium , now Alatri; whence, , , adj. , pertaining to Aletrium , Cic. Clu. 16 . — , the inhabitants of Aletrium , Cic. Clu. 20 ; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63 .— Also, , , the same: foederatus, Cic. Balb. 22 dub.

ălĕtūdo.opening: alo , fatness , = corporis pinguedo, Fest. p. 23 .

Ăleuas.opening: , = Ἀλεύας . A tyrant of Larissa , slain by his own servants , Ov. Ib. 321 and 509 Merk.— A worker in bronze , Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 86 .

Ălĕus.opening: adj. : Alea Minerva, the Alean or Alic Minerva , so called either from Aleus, king of Arcadia, or from Alea, a town in that country, Stat. Th. 4, 288 .

Ălexămĕnus.opening: , = Ἀλεξαμενός , a leader of the Ætolians , Liv. 35, 24 .

Ălexander.opening: Ἀλέξανδρος, hence, Charis. 64 P. asserts that there is also a nom. Alexandrus, but gives no example , the name of many persons of antiquity; among whom, The most renowned is Alexander , son of Philip and Olympia ,…

Ălexandrēa.opening: (the form of Cicero's time, Cic. Phil. 2, 19 ; id. Fin. 5, 19 ; Prop. 4, 10, 33 ( Alexandria , Müll.); Hor. C. 4, 14, 35 K. and H.; also under the Empire; so, Antiochēa and Antiochīa; cf. Prisc. p. 588 P., Ochsn. Eclog.…

ălexĭpharmăcon.opening: , = ἀλεξιφάρμακον , an antidote for poison , only in Plin. 21, 20, 84, § 146 .

ălĭbī.opening: adv. contr. from aliubi; aliusibi , elsewhere. Elsewhere , otherwhere , somewhere else , in or at another place , = alio loco, ἄλλοθι (very freq. in the post-Aug. per., esp. in Pliny; in Cic. only twice, and then in…

ălĭbĭlis.opening: adj. alo , affording nourishment , nutrilious , nourishing (perh. only in Varr.): lac, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 2 : casei, id. ib. 2, 11, 2 , § 3.— Pass. of that which readily grows or fattens: ita pulli alibiliores fiunt,…

ălĭca.opening: from alo, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 7 Müll.; akin to ἀλέω, ὀλαί acc. to Doed. , orig. adj. , nourishing , sc. farina. A kind of grain , spelt , Cato, R. R. 76 init. ; Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 50 .— Grits prepared from it ,…

ălĭcārĭus.opening: adj. alica , of or pertaining to spelt; hence, , , , one who grinds spelt : nemo est alicarius posterior te, Lucil. ap. Charis. p. 75 P.; and , , , a prostitute (as frequenting the place of the spelt-mills): alicariae…

ălĭcastrum.opening: , sc. frumentum [id.], a kind of spelt , summer-spelt (i. e. sown in the spring), Col. 2, 6 ; 2, 9 ; cf. Isid. Aug. 17, 3 .

ălĭcŭbi.opening: (earlier written , like neutrobi , acc. to Cassiod. Orth. 2314 P.; cf. Schne id. Gr. 1, 29 ), adv. aliquis-ubi , somewhere , anywhere , at any place , or in any thing (Inter alicubi et usquam hoc interest, quod alicubi…

ălĭcunde.opening: adv. , of place [aliquis-unde], from somewhere = ab aliquo loco, Gr. ἀμόθεν . Lit. : tu mihi aliquid aliquo modo alicunde ab aliquibus blatis, Plaut. Ep. 3, 1, 13 ; cf. verse 10: venit meditatus alicunde ex solo loco,…
